methodNote: Built 2026-08-05. We swept open listing portals town by town across every county within roughly 90 minutes of Raleigh — Movoto (MLS-fed) plus LandHub, LandCentury, and Landmodo — after the eight major land portals blocked automated collection. Every verified-live lot anchors to a live listing URL with price and acreage quoted verbatim; county of record is checked against county parcel GIS rather than the mailing address, with parcel or MLS numbers captured when the listing publishes them. County guides are lite-checked: corridor-level drive estimates and medians computed from this inventory alone. Listings move; each lot carries its own dated verification status.

knowledge.title: How tight is this market, really?
knowledge.html: 562 lots harvested; 370 are verified live today. The market prices by the minute. Wake runs $136,000 an acre inside 30 minutes. At 40 minutes, Johnston and Harnett run $65,000 to $70,000. At 45 to 55, Franklin, Chatham, and Granville sit at $30,000 to $40,000. Past the hour, Vance and Caswell fall under $20,000 and rural Moore under $10,000. Each step outward roughly halves the acre price. The value pockets: Granville, with volume at $30,000 an acre within 40 minutes of RTP; Franklin east of Louisburg; Vance if Kerr Lake fits the plan. Durham and Orange are thin because that land is built out or zoned away. Wake looks thin for a different reason: the big portals block automated collection, so more is for sale there than this inventory shows. These are asking prices from listings still live when we swept — fast sellers and off-market deals never enter a sample like this. Read these numbers as the market's shape, not its floor.

knowledge.title: "Perc" Is Slang — the Real Permit Chain
knowledge.html:
"Perc" Is Slang — the Real Permit Chain

Homeowners call it a "perc test." North Carolina's actual process is broader than that: a licensed evaluator examines the soil's texture, structure, and depth to the seasonal high water table across the site, not just how fast one hole drains. That evaluation leads to an Improvement Permit, issued by the county health department.

The Improvement Permit is not a green light to build whatever you want. It states a specific design wastewater flow — calculated at 120 gallons per day per bedroom — and a specific system type, standard or an alternative design if the soil is marginal. That number is what actually caps your house. A 5-acre lot with a permit rated for three bedrooms does not get you a five-bedroom house. The acreage is irrelevant once the flow number is set.

Before anyone pours concrete, you need a second document: an Authorization to Construct, issued once your installer's specific system design is approved against the permit.

  • A permit backed by a recorded plat is valid without expiration.
  • A permit backed only by a site plan is valid for five years, then it's dead — you start over.
  • If a seller hands you an old permit as proof the lot "perks," check which kind it is and whether the five years already ran out.

knowledge.title: The County Backlog — and the Legal Fast Lane
knowledge.html:
The County Backlog — and the Legal Fast Lane

Wake and Johnston counties are growing faster than their environmental health staff can keep up. Expect four to eight weeks just to get a county soil evaluation scheduled and completed. Johnston County's own posted number is five weeks or less, as of July 2026 — treat that as a floor, not a promise, and confirm current numbers before you write a due-diligence deadline into a contract.

State law gives you a private-sector way around the line. You can hire your own state-licensed soil scientist to perform the site evaluation instead of waiting in the county's queue. For the system design itself, a licensed professional engineer can prepare and seal the plans directly, and you can apply for your building permit as soon as you file a complete Notice of Intent to Construct — without waiting for the health department to finish its own review.

  • Private licensed soil scientist: typically 7 to 14 days.
  • County health department: typically 4 to 8 weeks.
  • The private path costs more upfront. If your due-diligence window is short, it's usually worth paying for.

knowledge.title: A Small Stream Can Erase Your Buildable Area
knowledge.html:
A Small Stream Can Erase Your Buildable Area

Large parts of Wake, Durham, and Johnston counties sit inside the Neuse River basin. Parts of Wake, Durham, and Chatham drain toward Jordan Lake. Both basins carry state riparian buffer rules, and the rules don't care that a stream looks small.

The buffer is measured 50 feet from the top of the bank, on both sides of the stream. It applies to intermittent streams — the kind that only run part of the year and can look like a dry ditch in July — not just the obvious year-round creek.

Do the math before you fall for a lot. A stream running through the middle of a parcel claims 50 feet on each bank: 100 feet of width gone. On a small or narrow lot, that can consume most of the usable ground even though the deed shows plenty of acreage. Get a buffer determination on the specific parcel — not a neighbor's, not a guess — before you're under contract.

knowledge.title: A Cheap Vacant Lot May Be a Buyout Parcel
knowledge.html:
A Cheap Vacant Lot May Be a Buyout Parcel

After Hurricane Matthew (2016) and Hurricane Florence (2018), North Carolina and FEMA bought out thousands of flood-prone properties, concentrated along the Neuse River corridor and in Cumberland County. The mechanics: the state buys the home at pre-storm fair market value, demolishes it, and deeds the land to local government with a permanent open-space restriction. FEMA covers 75% of the cost; the state covers 25%.

These parcels are never buildable again — not by you, not by whoever buys it after you. The restriction runs with the land forever, not with the owner who was there during the flood.

The tell: a vacant lot priced well under what nearby land is selling for, especially near a floodplain or a creek corridor. Before you get attached to a deal that looks too good, check the deed and the county's flood-buyout parcel records.

knowledge.title: The Well Is a Bet on What's Under That Spot
knowledge.html:
The Well Is a Bet on What's Under That Spot

City water is a guarantee. A private well is not. You're drilling into whatever rock sits under your specific lot, and two lots a quarter-mile apart can perform completely differently.

Parts of Wake, Durham, Chatham, and Lee counties sit inside the Triassic Basin — old rift-valley rock where groundwater collects in scattered fractures instead of one continuous aquifer. The state's own guidance for homeowners in this zone doesn't soften it: "Water well yields are typically very low, and many dry holes have been drilled." The same rock can hurt your septic chances too — the state notes soil at many Triassic sites "does not perform adequately during percolation tests."

Budget for the real range, not the best case. A completed residential well in North Carolina commonly runs $6,000 to $15,000, and geology decides where in that range you land — not the drilling company.

  • Get a well drilled, or at least get a hydrogeologic opinion on the specific lot, before closing.
  • Ask whether the property sits in a mapped Triassic basin zone before you assume a well will be cheap or reliable.

knowledge.title: Road Frontage Is Not a Driveway Permit
knowledge.html:
Road Frontage Is Not a Driveway Permit

Your deed showing frontage on a state route tells you nothing about whether you're allowed to cut a driveway there. Any new access point onto a state-maintained road needs its own NCDOT permit, separate from anything the county approves.

NCDOT evaluates that permit against minimum sight-distance standards: how far you can see down the road in both directions from the driveway location, checked against a design-vehicle table in NCDOT's own access policy. Driveway location, design, and construction have to meet the standards set by the district engineer, including those sight-distance requirements.

If a curve, a hill, or a tree line blocks that sight line at your only legal access point, NCDOT can deny the location outright, or approve it only on the condition that you build the fix — a turn lane, a wider shoulder, added pavement — at your own expense, not NCDOT's. Get a sight-distance check on the exact access point before you buy. A lot with beautiful frontage can still be a bad lot if the only legal driveway spot can't see far enough down the road.

knowledge.title: The Statewide Floor — What's True in Every County Below
knowledge.html:
"Perc test" is folklore. The real gate is a two-stage state permit.

Nobody in North Carolina legally "perc tests" a lot anymore — the phrase survives as slang for what's actually a licensed soil evaluation feeding a state-defined permit sequence under G.S. 130A, Article 11: an Improvement Permit (IP) confirming the site can support a wastewater system, then an Authorization to Construct (AC) issued after the county's field investigation confirms the specific installed design complies. The IP does not state an acreage — it locks in a design wastewater flow and system type sized to a specific facility (in practice, bedroom count), and that's what actually bounds the house, not the size of the parcel.

  • Non-expiring vs. dead-on-arrival: an Improvement Permit issued with a recorded plat is valid without expiration; one issued with only a site plan (no plat) is valid for five years and lapses if unused (G.S. 130A-335(f)). This is exactly why some older, pre-2010s vacant-lot permits quietly died and the lot needs a fresh evaluation under current rules, while a modern plat-documented IP survives indefinitely.
  • The private fast lane: a licensed professional engineer can issue an Engineered Option Permit (G.S. 130A-336.1), and a licensed soil scientist can qualify as an Authorized On-Site Wastewater Evaluator (G.S. 130A-336.2) — both bypass the county health department's own evaluation queue for a fee. This is the standard workaround when a county backlog runs multiple weeks, and it's worth pricing against just waiting.
  • The on-site wastewater program is still run by the Department of Health and Human Services, not DEQ (G.S. 130A-334(1f)) — DEQ owns water quality/buffer rules, DHHS owns septic.
  • Well construction runs a parallel process: private drinking-water wells need their own permit from the same local health department, under authority delegated by G.S. 87-97 and 15A NCAC 02C — "no person shall construct a private drinking water well without first obtaining a well construction permit from the local health department."

There is no family-subdivision exemption

This is the single most expensive myth circulating about NC land. "I'm just carving off an acre for my kid" does not exempt a division from full subdivision review. G.S. 160D-802 lists exactly five exemptions from local subdivision/plat requirements, and family transfer isn't one of them: (1) recombining previously recorded lots without increasing the lot count; (2) dividing land into parcels greater than 10 acres with no street right-of-way dedication; (3) public acquisition of strips for street widening or transportation corridors; (4) dividing a single-ownership tract of 2 acres or less into no more than three lots with no street right-of-way dedication; (5) dividing a tract under a probated will or intestate succession. Carve a 1-acre lot off a 5-acre tract for a relative and none of these apply unless the whole tract exceeds 10 acres with no new road, or the transfer happens through an estate.

Heirs property: NC has not passed what many guides assume it has

Correction worth flagging directly: North Carolina has not enacted the Uniform Partition of Heirs Property Act as of August 2026. An earlier attempt, House Bill 367 (2021), passed the House 80-28 and then died in a Senate committee. The current attempt, House Bill 976 / Senate Bill 317 (2025-2026 session, amending Chapter 46A §§26 and 87-99), was filed April 2025 and remained re-referred to the House Rules committee as of its last recorded action — it is not law. NC's Chapter 46A contains only ordinary partition procedure (Article 2, G.S. 46A-20 through 46A-86) — no mandatory-appraisal, kin-preference, or right-of-first-refusal protections for co-tenant heirs. Practically, this means heirs property — land inherited by multiple descendants as tenants in common, common on cheap multi-generational rural acreage — still resolves through an ordinary partition action: every heir must be located and joined, courts default toward sale unless in-kind division is proven workable, and a forced open-market sale is a live risk without the protections roughly half the country's states now guarantee their heirs-property owners. Budget months for title work and treat an attorney as mandatory, not optional.

NCDOT driveway permits: road frontage isn't access

Frontage tells you a driveway permit is possible, not that one is approved. Access onto a state-maintained road runs through NCDOT's Policy on Street and Driveway Access, reviewed first for sight distance in both directions from the proposed driveway. NCDOT's authority to require dedicated turn lanes, storage lanes, or additional right-of-way dedication when a project's traffic volume crosses defined thresholds comes from G.S. 136-18(29) — and hitting those thresholds on a busier NC route can mean a five-figure turn-lane condition attached to what looked like a routine driveway permit. Confirm the permit directly with NCDOT before treating "has frontage on a state road" as "is buildable."

Present-Use Value: the rollback bomb hiding in cheap acreage

Present-Use Value (PUV) values qualifying farm, horticultural, or forest land at its use value instead of market value — it's a large part of why some rural acreage in this footprint carries a tax bill that looks absurdly low. The catch is G.S. 105-277.4(c): when the land is disqualified — cleared, converted, subdivided out of the qualifying tract, built on beyond the excluded homesite — "the deferred taxes for the preceding three fiscal years are due and payable," plus interest. Ask the seller or the county tax office directly whether a parcel currently carries a PUV deferral before treating the listed tax bill as what ownership will actually cost once you build.

How the deal itself closes

  • NC is an attorney-closing state — a licensed NC attorney must conduct or directly supervise the closing, including the title search; there's no title-company-only closing here.
  • Vacant land uses its own form, NC REALTORS® Form 12-T (Offer to Purchase and Contract – Vacant Lot/Land), not the standard residential Form 2-T.
  • The due diligence fee, where used, goes directly to the seller — not escrow — and is non-refundable if the buyer walks; current form language gives the buyer until the end of the next banking day after the effective date to pay it, or they're in breach (seller terminates via Form 355-T).
  • Unimproved land is exempt from the Residential Property and Owners' Association Disclosure Statement — the statute (G.S. 47E-1) only reaches property with a dwelling on it. A seller can offer one voluntarily; nothing requires it.
  • The Mineral and Oil and Gas Rights Mandatory Disclosure Statement carries the identical vacant-land exemption — owners of vacant real estate with no residential dwelling don't have to provide it. That means a bare-land buyer gets zero statutory heads-up on severed mineral, oil, gas, or timber rights and is relying entirely on the closing attorney's title search to catch a severance that happened decades ago.

knowledge.title: Wake County
knowledge.html:
Permit authority and portal

Wake County's Wastewater Program (Environmental Services / Onsite Water Protection) issues septic and well permits; Wake County Planning, Development & Inspections handles zoning. Applications and inspection scheduling run through the county's EnerGov-based self-service portal rather than paper-only intake.

Wait-time reality

Wake doesn't publish a fixed turnaround figure, but independent septic-industry guides tracking the county tell buyers to plan on "four to eight weeks or longer" for a new-installation Improvement Permit, stretching to "several weeks to potentially several months in the permitting queue, particularly for complex sites or during busy building seasons" — against a volume of roughly 3,500 applications a year. That's the multi-week reality behind Wake's reputation, driven by it being the fastest-growing large county in this footprint. Simple repair permits move faster, sometimes within days.

Zoning families that allow site-built single-family

Unincorporated Wake runs a density ladder of straight residential districts, all permitting single-family detached homes: R-80/R-80W (very-low-density, 0.5 du/acre), R-40/R-40W (1.0 du/acre), R-30 — the prevailing rural classification at 1.45 du/acre — down through R-20, R-15, R-10, and R-5 closer to municipal utilities. The number in each district name is the nominal minimum lot size in thousands of square feet under conventional development.

Typical minimum lot size on septic

As everywhere in NC, soil evaluation — not a zoning table — sets the real minimum. In practice, R-40/R-30 zoning plus the soil area a 3-4 bedroom conventional system and its repair area need keeps most unincorporated Wake septic lots in the roughly 1-acre-plus range, climbing further on Triassic-basin soils (below).

Water/sewer availability pattern

Municipal water/sewer covers Raleigh, Cary, Wake Forest, Apex, and the other towns plus their extraterritorial fringes; unincorporated Wake outside those service areas is well-and-septic by default. Aqua North Carolina, a private regulated utility, also serves pockets of Wake where no municipal system reaches — worth checking before assuming "no city water" means "drill a well." Growth-corridor towns are raising rates hard to fund capacity: Fuquay-Varina adopted a 15% water and sewer rate increase for FY2026, and Holly Springs — which leans on emergency interconnections with Fuquay-Varina, Apex, and Cary rather than unlimited capacity of its own — is funding expansion through a $139 million FY2026-27 budget. A tap-fee number quoted a year ago is not this year's number in this corridor.

PUV prevalence

Wake is the most urbanized county in this guide, so PUV-enrolled farm/forest tracts are the exception rather than the rule — but they persist on the fringes toward the Johnston and Franklin lines, and the same three-year rollback (G.S. 105-277.4(c)) applies there as anywhere else.

Regional overlay risks specific to Wake

  • Neuse River riparian buffer: Wake sits at the head of the Neuse basin (Falls Lake and its tributaries). NC's riparian buffer rule requires a vegetated buffer along intermittent and perennial streams, lakes, and reservoirs across the basin (15A NCAC 02B .0233) — a stream that wasn't obvious from the road can erase a meaningful share of a small lot's buildable envelope. Get a formal stream/buffer determination before counting on the whole parcel.
  • Triassic Basin well risk: Wake is one of eleven counties on the Deep River Triassic basin per NC's Geological Survey. The underlying rock is clay-rich sandstone and siltstone with minimal pore space — well yield is unpredictable statewide in this formation, and "many dry holes have been drilled." This band runs through southern and western Wake toward the Chatham and Lee lines.

knowledge.title: Johnston County
knowledge.html:
Permit authority and portal

Johnston County Environmental Health issues septic and well permits; Public Utilities handles municipal water/sewer connections. The county runs a genuinely useful online permit-status lookup — searchable by address, street, or permit number — so a buyer can verify an existing permit before closing.

Wait-time reality

Johnston is the most transparent county in this set about its own backlog. Its Environmental Health department posted, in its own words: "the current Septic and Well response time is 5 weeks or less as of July1st, 2026." That's a real, dated, five-week queue — not an estimate — even as the county's own reporting shows residential construction activity cooling in the first half of 2026.

Zoning families that allow site-built single-family

Unlike Wake's density ladder, Johnston runs a single countywide residential district: "Currently, Johnston County has a single residential zoning district, Agricultural Residential (AR)." AR is intended, in the ordinance's own language, "to encourage the continuance of agricultural uses as well as to ensure that residential development will occur at sufficient densities to provide for a range of housing opportunities throughout the county," and it covers the large majority of unincorporated Johnston, permitting both farming and single-/two-family residential development. A more graduated district system has been proposed but was not in force as of this research.

Typical minimum lot size on septic

Same statewide rule: the health department's soil evaluation, not the AR zoning minimum, is the actual gate. AR's lot standards are built around what a conventional septic system plus repair area needs, which in practice keeps unincorporated Johnston lots around an acre or more outside town utility areas.

Water/sewer availability pattern

Capacity is tightening, not loosening. The Board of Commissioners voted in August to raise system development (tap) fees to their full calculated amount rather than phase them in, explicitly to protect roughly $8 million earmarked for capacity projects. The county is also studying regionalizing its water/sewer utility with neighboring systems. A pending state bill, S758 (2025-2026 session), would bar local governments from withholding water/sewer allocation from a project when capacity is actually available — itself a signal that allocation, not just tap fees, is a live fight here.

PUV prevalence

Johnston remains heavily agricultural outside its US-70/I-40 growth corridor, and PUV-enrolled farmland is common on the county's eastern and southern acreage — the same G.S. 105-277.4(c) rollback applies the moment that land is cleared for a house.

Regional overlay risk

Johnston sits within the Neuse River basin, so the same 50-foot riparian buffer rule constraining Wake applies here too, especially along the Neuse itself near Smithfield and Clayton — and Johnston's stretch of the Neuse carries its own flood history from Hurricanes Matthew and Florence, the same storms behind the buyout programs detailed in the Outer Ring section.

knowledge.title: Harnett County
knowledge.html:
Permit authority and portal

Harnett County Central Permitting is a genuine one-stop intake covering Environmental Health (septic/well), E-911 addressing, the Fire Marshal's Office, Inspections, Planning, and Harnett Regional Water. Permit status and inspection scheduling run through the county's eTRAKiT portal; septic/well applications themselves are still submitted as PDF attachments direct to Central Permitting rather than a full self-service upload.

Wait-time reality

Harnett doesn't publish a standing turnaround figure the way Johnston does. The eTRAKiT portal's own language promises the county "makes every effort to keep the scheduled time frames for inspections" — a courtesy statement, not a number. Treat Harnett as county-typical multi-week rather than assume it's faster than its Triangle-adjacent neighbors just because it's less urbanized.

Zoning families that allow site-built single-family

Harnett runs a Residential-Agricultural ladder — RA-40, RA-30, RA-20M, and RA-20R — confirmed on the county's own zoning maps; all permit single-family site-built homes plus agricultural use, and RA-20M additionally allows manufactured home parks. Dimensional requirements (minimum lot size, setbacks) sit in a dedicated ordinance section (§153.093) that steps down as the district number decreases.

Typical minimum lot size on septic

Same statewide principle: soil evaluation sets the real minimum. Third-party zoning summaries describe RA-30 as carrying roughly a one-acre minimum lot size with 150-foot minimum frontage, and RA-40 as requiring more than an acre per dwelling — treat these as directionally reliable but confirm the current ordinance text before relying on an exact figure.

Water/sewer availability pattern

Harnett Regional Water is the county's own utility, serving the Lillington/US-421 growth corridor with expanding service areas; land off that corridor is well-and-septic by default. Because HRW is a single county-owned system rather than a patchwork of small town utilities, whether a specific parcel can actually get service is a real question to confirm rather than assume from proximity to Lillington.

PUV prevalence

Harnett is one of the more PUV-heavy counties in this set — cheap-looking acreage away from the US-401/US-421 corridors is commonly enrolled in farm or forestry use-value, and the three-year G.S. 105-277.4(c) rollback is a real cost to model before clearing land to build.

knowledge.title: Franklin County
knowledge.html:
Permit authority and portal

Franklin County Environmental Health handles on-site water protection (septic and well); a county zoning permit is a prerequisite before an environmental health application is even accepted, and applications run through the county's Viewpoint Cloud portal. A searchable online permit database covers records issued since 2018, with older records added incrementally — a pre-2018 permit may still require a direct records request.

Wait-time reality

Franklin doesn't publish a turnaround figure, and given the county's lower growth pressure than Wake or Johnston, its queue is the least-documented of this deep-dive set. Budget the same multi-week statewide norm and confirm current timing directly with Environmental Health rather than assume.

Zoning families that allow site-built single-family

Franklin gates residential building behind zoning first — the county explicitly requires a zoning permit before it will accept the septic application — so confirming district and permitted use is the first step, not an afterthought, before assuming a rural tract is buildable.

Typical minimum lot size on septic

Soil evaluation is the real constraint, as everywhere in NC; Franklin's rural residential-agricultural zoning is calibrated to conventional septic lot sizes typical of the region — roughly an acre and up outside the towns.

Water/sewer availability pattern

Franklin is overwhelmingly well-and-septic outside Louisburg, Youngsville, Bunn, and Franklinton — the towns with their own municipal systems — and outside Wake County's northward-extending utility fringe near the Wake line.

PUV prevalence

Franklin sits squarely in the cheap-rural-acreage band this guide is warning about generally: PUV-enrolled farm and forest land is common away from US-1 and the Wake County line, and the same three-year-plus-interest rollback applies the moment qualifying use stops.

Regional overlay risk

Franklin straddles the Neuse and Tar-Pamlico basins depending on where in the county a parcel sits — confirm which basin (and which buffer rule) actually governs a specific stream rather than assume Neuse's rule automatically applies countywide.

knowledge.title: Durham County
knowledge.html:
Permit authority and portal

Durham County Public Health's Environmental Health Division issues septic and well permits; zoning runs through the consolidated city-county Unified Development Ordinance (UDO), in place since 2006. Septic/well records requests and applications route through the department's own forms rather than a unified EnerGov-style self-service portal for environmental health specifically.

Wait-time reality

Durham doesn't publish a turnaround figure on its Environmental Health pages; treat it as multi-week and confirm directly, the same caution as Franklin and Harnett.

Zoning families that allow site-built single-family

Durham's UDO residential districts run from RR (Residential Rural) — the district that actually reaches unincorporated county land, established "to provide for agricultural activities and residential development" at rural densities — down through RS-20 and RS-10 (20,000- and 10,000-square-foot lots) as land approaches the city.

Typical minimum lot size on septic

Durham is one of the few counties in this set where the ordinance states the number outright for conventional subdivisions: RR-district lots outside rural-tier watershed areas carry a 30,000-square-foot (about 0.69-acre) conventional minimum. For conservation subdivisions on individual septic, the UDO instead defers directly to the County Health Department's approval of suitable lot area rather than a fixed number — a clean textbook example of soil evaluation actually overriding a zoning minimum.

Water/sewer availability pattern

Durham's municipal system reaches deep into the county given the consolidated city-county structure, but unincorporated fringe land — north toward Granville and Person, east toward Wake — still runs well-and-septic. Durham's own environmental health fee schedule calls out parcels over 2 acres as requiring evaluation by a certified soil scientist rather than the standard county process, a useful marker of how the county treats larger rural tracts differently.

PUV prevalence

Durham is the second-most-urbanized county in this deep-dive set after Wake, so PUV land concentrates on the county's rural fringes rather than throughout.

Regional overlay risks

  • Neuse basin buffer rules apply across Durham's Neuse-tributary streams feeding Falls Lake.
  • Jordan Lake basin buffer rules apply on Durham's western/southwestern streams draining toward the Haw River/Jordan Lake watershed.
  • Triassic Basin well/septic risk applies statewide-confirmed for Durham as one of the eleven Deep River basin counties.

A single Durham parcel can plausibly sit in two different buffer regimes depending which side of the county's basin divide it falls on — get a formal DEQ stream/buffer determination rather than guess from a basin map.

knowledge.title: Orange County
knowledge.html:
Permit authority and portal

Orange County Environmental Health (Health Department) issues septic and well permits through the county's online Form Center. Orange also runs a broader Permitting Information Portal (PIP) for development-services permits generally, which the county itself describes as still being built out.

Wait-time reality

No published turnaround figure; treat as multi-week and confirm directly given growth pressure radiating from Chapel Hill and Hillsborough.

Zoning families that allow site-built single-family

Orange's UDO (covering the planning jurisdiction outside municipal limits) runs Rural Buffer (RB) — explicitly zoned to "provide for development at very low densities relying on individual wells and ground absorption systems" — alongside Agricultural Residential and Rural Residential (R-1). All three permit site-built single-family homes and share baseline setbacks (roughly 40 feet from the road right-of-way, 20 feet off each side and rear line, per third-party setback compilations — confirm against the current UDO text).

Typical minimum lot size on septic

Orange County's own guidance states this plainly: "a typical 4-bedroom septic system and repair area usually need ¼ to ⅓ of an acre of suitable soil" — that's the soil footprint alone, before RB/AR zoning minimums, setbacks, and well-isolation distances stack on top. Orange also lays out its Improvement Permit → Construction Authorization → well-permit sequence explicitly on its own septic-systems page, one of the clearer public explanations of the state process found across this entire set of counties.

Water/sewer availability pattern

OWASA (Orange Water and Sewer Authority) serves Chapel Hill and Carrboro; Hillsborough runs its own system. Unincorporated county land outside those boundaries — most of rural Orange — is well-and-septic, reinforced directly by the Rural Buffer district's zoning intent, which exists specifically to keep large swaths of the county on individual wells rather than extend utilities.

PUV prevalence

Rural Orange (west and north of Hillsborough, away from Chapel Hill) carries meaningful PUV-enrolled forest and farmland, consistent with the Rural Buffer district's whole purpose of preserving low-intensity land use.

Regional overlay risk

Orange straddles both the Jordan Lake watershed (New Hope Creek and other tributaries draining south toward the lake) and Cape Fear/Haw River drainage, so Jordan Lake's riparian buffer rule is a live constraint on a meaningful share of the county's streams — get a buffer determination before assuming a wooded creek line in listing photos is just landscaping.

knowledge.title: Chatham County
knowledge.html:
Permit authority and portal

Chatham County Public Health's Division of Environmental Health handles wastewater/septic and well permitting and monitoring; Chatham County Planning handles zoning, currently mid-rewrite through the "Recode Chatham" project replacing the county's legacy zoning ordinance with a new Unified Development Ordinance. Building/development permits run through an online portal the county launched in 2021.

Wait-time reality

No published turnaround figure was available from the county's own pages at research time — confirm current queue length directly with Environmental Health. Treat Chatham's timeline with real caution regardless of what any published number says: the county's growth story has leaned heavily on two industrial megasites, and megasite-driven housing demand is exactly what produces sudden environmental-health backlogs.

The VinFast reality check

Land pitches leaning on "Chatham is about to boom" deserve a second look right now. VinFast's roughly 2,000-acre Chatham County megasite promised production starting mid-2026 in exchange for close to $400 million in state and local incentives. The automaker missed its construction and hiring deadlines; North Carolina sued to reclaim the site; and Chatham County terminated its incentives deal with VinFast in late July 2026 after the company failed to meet those deadlines. Wolfspeed's project remains active, and the county's own 2026 development briefing points to a $390 million regional water infrastructure merger tied to serving these megasites — but the VinFast leg of the growth story has collapsed for now, and land marketing still leaning on it is behind the news.

Zoning families that allow site-built single-family

Chatham's legacy ordinance (still in force during the Recode rewrite) runs Rural Agricultural (RA) and related conservation/residential districts permitting site-built single-family homes on individual well and septic across most of the unincorporated county. Expect district names and standards to change as Recode Chatham's new UDO is adopted — reconfirm a parcel's zoning close to the time of purchase rather than trusting an older listing.

Typical minimum lot size on septic

As statewide, soil evaluation is the actual constraint; Chatham's clay-heavy Triassic-basin soils (below) push effective septic lot sizes upward in the affected part of the county specifically.

Water/sewer availability pattern

Chatham is overwhelmingly well-and-septic outside Pittsboro, Siler City, and the fringes reaching across the Wake County line toward Cary/Apex — reinforced by the same $390 million regional water infrastructure push tied to the megasite corridor, which is extending service toward the industrial sites but not broadly across the county's rural land.

PUV prevalence

Chatham carries substantial PUV-enrolled forestland and farmland, especially west of Pittsboro and around Siler City — exactly the kind of "cheap acreage" this guide keeps flagging, where the G.S. 105-277.4(c) three-year rollback needs checking before assuming the listed tax bill is the real number.

Regional overlay risks

  • Jordan Lake watershed buffer: Chatham contains Jordan Lake itself, so the riparian buffer rule (commonly cited at roughly 50 feet from the stream, 15A NCAC 02B .0267) touches a large share of the county's streams and shoreline-adjacent land — this is the single county in this guide where that rule is most likely to actually bite.
  • Triassic Basin: Chatham is one of the eleven Deep River basin counties — clay-rich sandstone/siltstone, unpredictable well yield, unreliable drainfield performance.

knowledge.title: Granville County
knowledge.html:
Permit authority and portal

Granville County's environmental health function is run jointly with neighboring Vance County as Granville-Vance Public Health, a merged district — septic and well permits for Granville parcels come out of that shared division rather than a Granville-only department. Fees were last revised effective July 1, 2025 (lot evaluation $400 conventional / $450 pump-system, well permit $460). Zoning permits run separately through Granville County Planning & Zoning.

Wait-time reality

No published turnaround figure; confirm directly with Granville-Vance Public Health, given the shared district serves two counties' worth of demand from one office.

Zoning families that allow site-built single-family

Granville's rural zoning includes an Agricultural-Residential district (AR-40, among others) permitting site-built single-family homes across most of the unincorporated county; as with Harnett's RA districts, the "-40" naming signals a roughly 40,000-square-foot nominal minimum.

Typical minimum lot size on septic

Same statewide rule, stated plainly by a local land-buyer guide covering the county: "There is no universal minimum lot size for a septic system. The soil and layout of your specific site drive what is possible and what type of system is required." AR-40 zoning's nominal acre-plus minimum is calibrated around that reality, not the other way around.

Water/sewer availability pattern

Granville is overwhelmingly well-and-septic outside Oxford and Creedmoor — the county's two municipal systems — and outside Wake/Durham's northward utility fringe near those county lines.

PUV prevalence

Granville is one of the more PUV-dense counties in this set: large tracts of enrolled farmland and managed forestland are common away from US-15/US-96. The tax-bill-looks-cheap trap this guide keeps flagging is especially live here — check PUV status with the county tax office before assuming the listed tax number survives a build.

Regional overlay risk

Granville is one of the eleven Deep River Triassic-basin counties per NC's Geological Survey — the same clay-rich sandstone/siltstone well-yield and drainfield-reliability risk affecting Wake, Durham, and Chatham applies here too, and it's a real reason to budget for a well-yield contingency before committing to cheap Granville acreage.

knowledge.title: The Outer Ring — Nash, Wilson, Vance, Person, Warren, Lee, Moore, Wayne, Sampson, Cumberland, Hoke, Alamance
knowledge.html:
What doesn't change out here

Every rule in the statewide-floor section above — the Improvement Permit/Authorization to Construct sequence, no family-subdivision exemption, no enacted heirs-property protections, NCDOT driveway sight-distance and turn-lane exposure, PUV's three-year rollback, attorney-closing/Form 12-T/no-disclosure-on-vacant-land transaction mechanics — applies identically across all twelve of these counties. What changes is growth pressure, water/sewer reach, and which regional overlay risks are actually live.

Permit authority and structure

All twelve run the same basic model as the deep-dive eight: a county (or shared multi-county) Environmental Health division issues septic and well permits, and a separate Planning/Zoning or Inspections department handles land-use approval. Cumberland County explicitly requires the zoning permit in hand before Environmental Health will release the septic permit, and rolled out a new online "Citizen Connect" platform for permitting and environmental-health status in August 2025. Vance shares Granville-Vance Public Health with Granville (see above). Moore County splits the function across a dedicated Environmental Health division and a separate Planning & Inspections department administering its own Unified Development Ordinance.

Wait-time reality

None of these twelve publish a standing turnaround figure the way Johnston does. Growth pressure — and queue length with it — is genuinely uneven: Cumberland (Fayetteville/Fort Liberty) and Moore (Pinehurst/Southern Pines) carry real, sustained building demand and deserve the same multi-week caution as the deep-dive counties; Nash, Wilson, Warren, Vance, and Sampson are lower-growth and more likely to move faster, but "likely faster" is not a substitute for calling the county before writing a due-diligence-period clock into a contract.

Zoning families that allow site-built single-family

The same residential-agricultural naming pattern recurs across the ring — rural districts in Moore's and Cumberland's UDOs, Alamance's agricultural/residential districts, and equivalents in Lee, Wayne, Sampson, and the rest all carry a district permitting site-built single-family homes on individual well and septic as the default outside town limits. Confirm the specific district and its lot standards county by county rather than relying on the naming pattern alone.

Typical minimum lot size on septic

Identical statewide principle: soil evaluation drives what's buildable, not a zoning table. Expect the same practical range as the deep-dive counties — roughly an acre or more outside municipal utility service for a conventional system plus repair area, more on poor soils.

Water/sewer availability pattern

Municipal service concentrates around each county's towns — Fayetteville and Hope Mills in Cumberland; Pinehurst, Southern Pines, and Aberdeen in Moore; Sanford in Lee; Burlington, Graham, and Mebane in Alamance; Goldsboro in Wayne; Rocky Mount in Nash; Wilson in Wilson County. Everywhere else in the ring is well-and-septic by default, the same pattern as the deep-dive eight.

PUV prevalence

The outer ring is, county for county, the most agricultural part of this guide's footprint — Sampson, Wayne, Nash, Wilson, and Warren in particular are core Coastal Plain/upper-Piedmont farm-belt counties, and PUV-enrolled land is common rather than exceptional. The same G.S. 105-277.4(c) three-year-plus-interest rollback applies the instant qualifying land converts to a homesite.

Regional overlay risks concentrated in this ring

  • FEMA/state buyout parcels — the sharpest trap in this whole guide. Cumberland County absorbed one of North Carolina's highest concentrations of post-Hurricane-Matthew (2016) and Hurricane-Florence (2018) buyouts. Matthew alone caused "100,000 homes, businesses, and government buildings" damaged statewide, an estimated $4.8 billion in damage, and 26 deaths. North Carolina's Strategic Buyout Program (Rebuild NC, FEMA-funded) has since permanently acquired repeatedly-flooded Cumberland County properties, demolished the structures, and deed-restricted the land as open space forever. The same disaster-recovery pipeline approved buyouts for 185 Wayne County homeowners along the Neuse River corridor near Goldsboro, then identified 192 more (84 more approved in one later round) — over 270 homes total pulled permanently out of that corridor. These parcels do not stay flagged forever. A cleared, deed-restricted former-buyout lot can resurface years later as a "cheap vacant lot" listing with nothing in the photos to indicate the history. Before buying suspiciously cheap vacant land in Cumberland or Wayne County near the Little River, Cape Fear, or Neuse corridors, check the parcel against the county's buyout-property list and deed directly — a buyout deed restriction permanently bars rebuilding, full stop, no matter how the land is marketed.
  • Triassic Basin: Lee and Moore counties both sit within the same eleven-county Deep River Triassic basin as Wake/Chatham/Durham/Granville — identical well-yield and drainfield caution applies, and Lee County (Sanford) in particular has a documented history of groundwater study tied to this same basin geology.
  • Jordan Lake / Haw River buffer: Alamance County sits upstream of Jordan Lake on the Haw River, and the county confirms directly that the Jordan Lake riparian buffer rule is administered there by NC DEQ's Division of Water Resources — the same rule constraining Chatham, Durham, and Orange reaches into southern Alamance.
  • Neuse basin buffer: Wilson and Wayne counties sit within the Neuse basin (Wilson via Contentnea Creek, Wayne along the Neuse itself through Goldsboro), so the riparian buffer rule applies there too; Nash County sits primarily in the neighboring Tar-Pamlico basin, which carries its own parallel buffer rule rather than Neuse's.

knowledge.title: The Off-Market Playbook
knowledge.html:
The MLS shows you what a seller (or their agent) already decided to advertise. It does not show you the three heirs sitting on 40 acres they can't agree to sell, the timber company writing off a marginal tract, the county's tax-foreclosure docket, or the retired farmer who'd sell tomorrow if someone just knocked. Off-market land is not a trick or a shortcut — it's a different, slower search that trades convenience for price. Everything below is a real channel. None of them are a Saturday-afternoon activity.

County GIS: scout vacant parcels yourself

Every NC county publishes a public GIS parcel viewer as its own system of record — ownership, acreage, zoning, tax value, and often building footprints. Wake County's is iMAPS; Durham runs a parcel layer through its Open Data Portal at maps.durhamnc.gov; Johnston County runs MapClick. Chatham, Harnett, Franklin, Granville, and the rest of the state run the same idea under their own county GIS pages.

  • Filter for parcels with little or no building value on a large land value — that's raw or lightly-improved ground.
  • Cross-reference the tax-record owner's mailing address against the parcel address. An out-of-state or out-of-county mailing address is a strong signal of an absentee or inherited-and-forgotten owner.
  • Long ownership tenure (deed date decades back) plus no recent activity is the classic profile of a seller who has simply never been asked.
  • A polite letter or postcard to the tax-record owner, not a cold call, is the standard next move — this is a patient-capital search, not a hot-lead funnel.

Tax-foreclosure upset bids

Every NC county forecloses on delinquent parcels through the Superior Court, and the sale itself is a genuinely public, genuinely under-shopped process. Under the in rem tax foreclosure procedure, the court appoints a commissioner to conduct the sale, which is then advertised and run under the state's general judicial-sale rules. Once a bid is on record, anyone can file a higher bid within a 10-day upset-bid window — each new bid must beat the last by the greater of 5% or $750, and each successful upset bid resets the 10-day clock.

  • Filings and sale notices live with the Clerk of Superior Court's civil division and the county tax office — not on any real estate portal.
  • A sale can run for months as bids get upset repeatedly; the entry point (watching the docket) is public, but winning takes patience and a willingness to keep re-checking.
  • You are buying "as-is," with no title warranty from the court, and other liens can survive the sale — run a title check before you bid, not after you win.

Estate and probate

Real property that passes to heirs by a will or by intestate succession is exempt from local subdivision review when it's divided along the terms of the probate — the state doesn't force a probate division through the same plat-approval process as a commercial subdivision. That's good news for the heirs, but it also means estate land often sits in limbo for years while the estate stays open, because nobody wants to be the one to force a sale.

  • Open estates are public record with the Clerk of Superior Court's estates division — the file names the personal representative (executor/administrator).
  • Approach through the personal representative or their attorney, not by tracking down individual heirs — that's who actually has authority to negotiate a sale.
  • If the estate lists multiple heirs as co-owners rather than a single personal representative with sale authority, you may be looking at an heirs-property situation — see the warning below before you get attached to the deal.

Timber-company dispositions

Large industrial timberland owners with NC holdings periodically sell off tracts that no longer fit their portfolio. Weyerhaeuser's own language for this is that some of its land is "determined to have more value to other owners" and is moved through a network of local, independent real estate brokers rather than public retail listings. Rayonier runs the same playbook under its own portfolio-optimization language. The entry point is a relationship with a regional timberland broker, not a keyword search — firms like Carolina Timberland Sales work exactly this niche.

These tracts are frequently raw and unentitled, and they're disproportionately likely to be crossed by a stream — which means the riparian-buffer math below matters more here than almost anywhere else on this list.

Developer remnant lots, through the builder network

Every subdivision build-out leaves a handful of lots behind — retention-pond corners, oddly-shaped leftovers, a lot with a stormwater easement eating half the pad, a lot the builder just didn't want. These almost never get an individual public listing; they get worked off quietly through the builder's own circle: subcontractors, the grading contractor, and the local Home Builders Association chapter (part of the statewide NC Home Builders Association network of local HBAs). Showing up at local HBA events, or simply asking a civil engineer or site contractor who works new subdivisions, surfaces these lots long before — if ever — they hit a portal.

Expired listings

An MLS or Zillow search filtered to "expired" or "withdrawn" land listings surfaces sellers who already tried the open market and didn't get a deal done — a built-in motivated-seller signal, and pricing history you can actually use in a negotiation. Tools like REDX, Vulcan7, and PropStream exist specifically to pull contact information off expired/withdrawn listings. You don't need to be actively working a live listing with an agent to ask them to run this search for you.

Land-specialist agents worth calling

Most residential agents avoid land deals — lower commission on a lower price point, and none of the soil, buffer, access, or entitlement knowledge a raw-land deal actually requires. National land-focused brokerages operate across NC (National Land Realty, Mossy Oak Properties, Whitetail Properties, United Country, and independent regional timberland brokers among them), and their agents routinely carry private, unlisted relationships with landowners who don't want a yard sign — privacy, an active hunting lease, a tenant farmer mid-season. A good land agent has already pre-screened for most of the landmines in the second half of this playbook; that's what the commission buys.

The human channels — the honest note

Facebook land-buyer/seller groups (county- and region-specific), Facebook Marketplace, Craigslist, and Nextdoor all carry real inventory: landowners who would rather sell peer-to-peer and skip a commission entirely. This is genuinely one of the best sources of true off-market land in rural NC.

It is also not a search you can automate. Nobody builds you an API for a Facebook group. Someone — you, your builder, or someone you're paying — has to join the groups, watch the feed daily, and message a "3 acres, cash only, no survey" post the same day it goes up, because in a hot rural county these move within hours. There's no paperwork trail, no appraisal, and no agent's due-diligence habit built in — you bring all of that yourself. Treat it as a standing, low-tech habit, not an occasional search, and it will out-produce every portal on this list.

The heirs-property warning

Land that's stayed in one family for generations disproportionately means multiple heirs each hold an undivided fractional interest — no single heir can sign clear title to the whole parcel, no matter how friendly they are or how confidently they talk about "my land." North Carolina adopted the Uniform Partition of Heirs Property Act in 2020 (codified in Chapter 46A) specifically because heirs property was being lost to forced partition sales at a fraction of fair value. The Act now requires a court-ordered appraisal and gives the other co-tenants a structured buyout / right-of-first-refusal option before any partition sale — open-market or auction — can proceed.

For a buyer, the practical translation is blunt: an heirs-property tract can take months to clear even after every heir personally agrees to sell, an attorney is not optional, and "I bought it from the heir I know" is a claim on a fraction of the parcel — not the parcel.

The septic reality: what an Improvement Permit actually buys you

"Perc test" is the popular shorthand, but it isn't the legal sequence. North Carolina's actual process is soil evaluation → Improvement Permit (IP) → Construction Authorization (CA) — a three-tier permitting chain built around the Improvement Permit as its foundation. The IP doesn't just certify that the soil will "perc." It fixes a specific bedroom count and wastewater system type for that exact site, because the state sizes systems on a design daily flow of 120 gallons per day per bedroom. That number — not the acreage — is what actually bounds how big a house you can build. A three-bedroom IP doesn't quietly become a five-bedroom house without a new permitting cycle.

On expiration: current-generation Improvement Permits (issued under the rules effective January 1, 2024 onward) are managed through suspension or revocation for cause — a site change, an inactive application — rather than a flat calendar expiration. But any IP issued before that date keeps running under whatever the older rule set said when it was issued, and general industry guidance still describes older-vintage permits as carrying a five-year validity clock. Translation for a buyer: don't take a decades-old IP on faith. Pull the actual permit file from the county and confirm it's still active before you count on it.

The backlog, and the statutory fast path around it

Fast-growing county environmental health departments — Wake, Durham, and Mecklenburg among the most cited — routinely run behind on soil evaluations and IP issuance simply from new-construction volume; buyers regularly see the backlog add weeks to a closing timeline. There's a private-sector fast path around it: a licensed soil scientist or professional engineer can issue an Engineered Option Permit (EOP) directly, letting the owner file a Notice of Intent to Construct and pull a building permit without waiting in the county's IP queue. The legislature has since attached statutory turnaround times specifically to EOP applications. For a buyer working against a due-diligence deadline, this option is often the difference between closing on schedule and walking away from the deposit.

Riparian buffers can eat a small lot whole

Two overlapping rules bind a large share of the Triangle: the Neuse River Basin buffer rule and the Jordan Lake watershed buffer rule (15A NCAC 02B .0267, in force since 2009). Both impose a 50-foot vegetated buffer on each side of a stream — and critically, that reaches intermittent streams and unnamed wet-weather drainages, not just year-round named creeks. These rules bind Wake, Durham, Johnston, and Chatham counties among others, right through the built-up parts of the Triangle.

A "blue line" on a plat — or a feature that isn't even mapped yet — can consume most of a small lot's usable building envelope once the 50-foot setback on each bank and the septic repair-area reservation both eat into it. Never assume a wooded corner of a lot is "extra yard"; check whether it's a buffer.

FEMA buyout parcels: the suspiciously cheap lot

After Hurricanes Matthew (2016) and Florence (2018), federally funded buyout programs — run in NC through the state's ReBuild NC Strategic Buyout Program — purchased flood-prone homes, demolished the structures, and placed the land under a permanent open-space deed restriction. These parcels concentrate along the Neuse River corridor and in Cumberland County, and they resurface on the market, or in a GIS search, looking like an ordinary cheap vacant lot — because that's exactly what it now is on the surface. The deed restriction runs with the land in perpetuity: it cannot be built on again, period. Run a title search, or call the county floodplain administrator, before you fall for a cheap creekside lot that's a little too clean.

The Present-Use Value rollback

Some of the cheapest large-acreage listings in counties like Granville, Franklin, and Harnett are enrolled in Present-Use Value (PUV) — deferred taxation for actively farmed or forested land. The moment that land is disqualified (sold into a non-qualifying use, subdivided below the qualifying threshold, or simply taken out of farming or timber production), the deferred taxes for the preceding three fiscal years come due immediately, with interest, as a lien on the property. That rollback bill is a real transaction cost a "$3,000/acre" asking price never discloses on its face — ask the seller or the tax office for PUV status and an estimated rollback figure before assuming today's tax bill is tomorrow's.

NCDOT driveway permits: frontage isn't approval

Any connection to a state-maintained road requires an NCDOT driveway permit, evaluated against sight-distance standards in both directions from the proposed driveway location. A gorgeous lot on a curve or the crest of a hill can fail sight distance outright, forcing the driveway to a different, less convenient spot on the parcel — or getting it denied at that location entirely. On higher-traffic roads, NCDOT can also condition approval on the applicant funding a turn lane or other roadway improvement, a cost that is never baked into the land's asking price and can run substantial. "Has road frontage" on a listing means the parcel touches a road. It does not mean a driveway has been approved there — get the driveway permit feasibility checked before you count on the frontage.

The family-subdivision exemption that doesn't exist

A persistent myth in NC land circles: that you can freely carve up a large tract and hand pieces to family members without triggering subdivision review. There is no such exemption in North Carolina law. State statute lists exactly five categories exempt from local subdivision regulation:

  • Recombining already-subdivided, recorded lots without increasing the total lot count;
  • Dividing land into parcels greater than 10 acres with no new street right-of-way;
  • Public acquisition of road-widening or right-of-way strips;
  • Dividing a tract of 2 acres or less into no more than 3 lots, with no new right-of-way; and
  • Dividing a tract per the terms of a probated will or intestate succession.

"Give my son two acres off the back corner" doesn't fit any of the five. If a division doesn't land in one of those categories, it goes through the same subdivision process — and often the same road, stormwater, and utility standards — as a commercial developer's plat.

Triassic Basin ground: the well is a gamble, not a formality

Parts of Wake, Chatham, Lee, and Durham counties sit inside the Deep River Triassic Basin, a geologic formation with a well-earned reputation among NC drillers for unpredictable yield. A USGS baseline study across northwestern Lee and southeastern Chatham counties found well depths ranging from 26 to 720 feet and yields ranging from just 0.25 to 100 gallons per minute on similarly-sited wells. Because yield in this basin depends on hitting the right fracture in the underlying rock rather than a predictable water table, a neighbor's strong well is not a reliable predictor for your lot. Budget realistically — a private well in NC commonly runs $6,000 to $15,000 — and understand that in Triassic Basin ground, that number buys you a hole in the ground, not a guaranteed result. A low-yield or dry well means paying again for a redrill.

Water and sewer allocation: the tap fee is a moving target

Rural and suburban-fringe land routinely gets marketed "utilities available" when what's actually available is capacity someone has to apply for — and capacity is finite and shifting. Johnston County revised its system development fees and bulk sewer-capacity charges for the current fiscal year and runs a formal sewer-allocation policy that reserves large blocks of treatment capacity for specific uses, meaning a residential hookup request competes for what's left. Fuquay-Varina adopted a 15% combined water/sewer rate increase for the current fiscal year, with further increases already planned to fund capacity expansion — a trajectory worth building into any pro forma for land in that service area. Where there's no municipal system at all, Aqua North Carolina — a private utility regulated by the NC Utilities Commission — serves roughly 321,000 people across 51 NC counties, frequently in exactly the kind of rural subdivision where off-market land shows up. Its rates, and its willingness to extend service to a specific parcel, are separate questions from whether "water is on the road."

How an NC land deal actually gets papered

North Carolina requires a licensed attorney to close a real estate transaction — there is no escrow-company closing tradition here, and that cost belongs in your budget from the start. The standard vacant-land purchase agreement is a distinct form from the improved-residential contract, built specifically for unimproved lots, and it carries the same due-diligence-fee mechanic buyers see on houses: a negotiated sum paid directly to the seller — not held in trust — for the buyer's right to terminate during due diligence, and non-refundable except for a seller default. Treat it as the real cost of tying up a property, not a formality.

Vacant, unimproved land also falls entirely outside North Carolina's Residential Property Disclosure Act, which by its own terms only reaches property with one to four existing dwelling units. There is no statutory seller disclosure statement on a bare lot, and the voluntary vacant-land disclosure form the state's REALTOR association publishes is exactly that — voluntary, not required. That silence cuts against the buyer: nobody is legally obligated to volunteer the buffer, the PUV enrollment, or the septic system that failed evaluation five years ago. Finally, in the eastern counties especially, confirm you're buying the whole stick: North Carolina law lets a prior owner sever and separately convey or reserve mineral, oil and gas, or timber rights by deed, so the surface owner and the rights owner can be two entirely different parties. A title search is the only way to know before you close.

knowledge.title: Wake County — what the money buys
knowledge.html:
Wake County

Wake is the premium. Land runs about $136,000 an acre — the highest in this inventory — and the verified sample spans $69,000 for four-tenths of an acre in the fringe towns to $775,000 for seven acres near the city. Drives run 12 to 30 minutes, the shortest on this list. The one thing to know: county lines bleed. Listings with Fuquay-Varina, Holly Springs, Zebulon, and Wendell addresses regularly sit in Harnett, Franklin, or Johnston. We verify the county of record on every lot; do the same before you assume Wake schools and Wake taxes.

knowledge.title: Durham County — what the money buys
knowledge.html:
Durham County

Durham has little raw land left, and the price says so: about $75,000 an acre, behind only Wake and Orange. What exists is infill or the rural north around Bahama and Rougemont. Drives run 25 to 40 minutes to Raleigh, less to RTP. The one thing to know: a Durham mailing address is not Durham County. Nearly a third of the lots harvested under a Durham label actually sat in Person, Granville, or Orange — Durham parcel GIS had no record of them. Every Durham lot shown here passed the parcel check.

knowledge.title: Orange County — what the money buys
knowledge.html:
Orange County

Orange is Chapel Hill and Hillsborough money: about $116,000 an acre, on the thinnest close-in supply in this inventory. Drives run 20 to 30 minutes to Durham and RTP, 35 to 50 to Raleigh. The one thing to know: the scarcity is written into law. Rural-buffer zoning and watershed rules set large lot minimums and hold buildable supply down on purpose. A lot that is truly entitled to build earns its premium here. Confirm zoning and water rules before you go under contract.

knowledge.title: Chatham County — what the money buys
knowledge.html:
Chatham County

Chatham is two markets wearing one name. The Pittsboro and Chapel Hill side prices toward six figures an acre and rides Chatham Park and the VinFast corridor. West and south toward Siler City and Bear Creek, the county median falls to $35,000 an acre, and four acres for $150,000 is normal. Drives run 35 to 55 minutes. The one thing to know: nearly everything here builds on well and septic, so the soil evaluation decides what a lot is worth. Price the perc test into every offer.

knowledge.title: Johnston County — what the money buys
knowledge.html:
Johnston County

Johnston is the workhorse: about $65,000 an acre median, with real spread — under $100,000 buys a town-edge lot, $195,000 buys 2.6 acres, and the Clayton side prices like Wake spillover. Drives run 25 to 45 minutes. The one thing to know: the same dollar doubles its acreage south of I-95. Clayton, Archer Lodge, and Wilson's Mills carry the commuter premium; Four Oaks, Benson, and Kenly sell the same dirt for half. Decide which half of the county you are buying before you shop.

knowledge.title: Harnett County — what the money buys
knowledge.html:
Harnett County

Harnett carries the deepest single-county count in this inventory, and its $70,000-an-acre median tells you what happened: northern Harnett is now Raleigh commuter belt. Angier, the Fuquay fringe, and Lillington price as Wake spillover, 40 to 60 minutes out. The one thing to know: the cheap Harnett of five years ago moved south. Below Lillington, toward Bunnlevel and Spring Lake, acreage money stretches again — and the south end answers to Fort Bragg's economy, not Raleigh's. Know which gravity you are buying into.

knowledge.title: Franklin County — what the money buys
knowledge.html:
Franklin County

Franklin is the closest true land value to Raleigh: about $40,000 an acre, 30 to 50 minutes out on US-1 and NC-96. The one thing to know: the price gradient is steep. Youngsville sits against Wake Forest and prices like it; Franklinton is the middle; Louisburg and everything east sells country acreage at country prices. The same $160,000 buys one Youngsville acre or four acres past Louisburg. County water reaches some corridors and not others, so confirm water and septic parcel by parcel.

knowledge.title: Granville County — what the money buys
knowledge.html:
Granville County

Granville holds the most listings in this inventory and one of its best ratios: about $30,000 an acre, with the south end — Creedmoor, Butner, Stem — 30 to 40 minutes from RTP on I-85. Three to five acres for $100,000 to $150,000 is the standing offer. The one thing to know: the county runs on a north-south price slope. South of Oxford you pay commuter money; north toward Stovall and Bullock the same acreage costs a third less. Stem-area zips straddle the Durham line, so check the county of record.

knowledge.title: Vance County — what the money buys
knowledge.html:
Vance County

Vance is the cheapest meaningful supply inside an hour: about $19,000 an acre, 50 to 60 minutes up US-1 and I-85 around Henderson and Kittrell. Five acres for under $100,000 is routine here. The one thing to know: Kerr Lake sets the local hierarchy. Tracts near the lake and its access roads price above the county median and hold their value; Henderson infill prices below it. If the plan is acreage and a boat, Vance is the strongest dollar on this list.

knowledge.title: Person County — what the money buys
knowledge.html:
Person County

Person prices at about $24,000 an acre around Roxboro, 55 to 70 minutes up US-501, with Hyco and Mayo lakes as the local draw. The one thing to know: this county entered our inventory by accident. Its handful of lots were harvested under Durham labels and re-filed here after the parcel check — nobody has swept Person on purpose yet. The price is real; the selection is not representative. A dedicated Person sweep is on the work list, and asking for it moves it up.

knowledge.title: Nash County — what the money buys
knowledge.html:
Nash County

Nash sells land at about $26,000 an acre, 45 to 60 minutes east on US-64 around Nashville, Spring Hope, and Middlesex. Four acres for $100,000 is the shape of the market. The one thing to know: the county's west edge moves first. The Middlesex side sits closest to Zebulon and catches Wake's growth wave years before the Rocky Mount side does. Our sample here is nine lots — enough to price the county, not enough to map it street by street.

knowledge.title: Wilson County — what the money buys
knowledge.html:
Wilson County

Wilson runs about $27,000 an acre, 50 to 65 minutes out US-264 and I-587, on a small sample of eight lots. The one thing to know: Wilson owns its own fiber utility. Greenlight, the municipal broadband network, gives this county better internet than almost anywhere else on this list — a real difference when the build includes working from home. Land money here behaves like Nash: flat, steady, priced by the acre and not by the school district.

knowledge.title: Alamance County — what the money buys
knowledge.html:
Alamance County

Alamance sells at about $29,000 an acre and sits on the seam between the Triangle and the Triad. Raleigh is 60 to 75 minutes, but Durham and Chapel Hill are 35 to 45 — Mebane is the commuter play. The one thing to know: the county prices east to west. Mebane's boom reaches east-county land first; toward Burlington and past it, the same money buys noticeably more. Ten lots is a modest sample; the direction of the price slope is not in doubt.

knowledge.title: Caswell County — what the money buys
knowledge.html:
Caswell County

Caswell is the cheapest county in this inventory: about $16,500 an acre around Yanceyville, 75 to 90 minutes out. The one thing to know: no interstate touches Caswell, and none is coming. That is why the land is cheap and why it stays quiet — tobacco country, hardwood, long road frontage, neighbors measured in fields. Buy here for acreage and silence, with Danville and Burlington as the errand towns, and check broadband availability address by address before you commit.

knowledge.title: Moore County — what the money buys
knowledge.html:
Moore County

Read the median first: $9,000 an acre. That number tells you these lots are not in Pinehurst. The Moore lots in this inventory sit in the county's rural north — Robbins, High Falls, Eagle Springs country — 60 to 75 minutes out, where timber and pasture set the price. The golf belt twenty minutes south is a different planet and does not appear here. The one thing to know: this is the cheapest dirt on the list, and the drive is the reason. Buy it for acreage, not for commute.

knowledge.title: Cumberland County — what the money buys
knowledge.html:
Cumberland County

Cumberland is a Fayetteville market, not a Raleigh one. Land runs about $54,500 an acre, and the 60-to-75-minute drive to Raleigh is beside the point — demand here answers to Fort Bragg. The one thing to know: military turnover is the engine. It keeps resale liquid and rentals strong, and it means the buyer pool for a finished house refills every transfer season. If the household works in the Triangle, look north instead; this commute will not soften.

knowledge.title: Hoke County — what the money buys
knowledge.html:
Hoke County

Hoke runs about $35,000 an acre around Raeford, and it grows on Fort Bragg spillover, not Raleigh commuting — Raleigh is 75 to 90 minutes and beside the point here. The one thing to know: the Sandhills work in your favor. Sandy soil percs readily, so septic approval — the step that kills lots elsewhere — usually passes here. Confirm it anyway, then expect approval. Seventeen lots give this county a fair read: modest money, easy soil, Bragg-anchored demand.

knowledge.title: Wayne County — what the money buys
knowledge.html:
Wayne County

Wayne runs about $28,500 an acre around Goldsboro, 60 to 75 minutes southeast. Demand here anchors to Seymour Johnson Air Force Base the way Cumberland's anchors to Fort Bragg — steady, military, local. The one thing to know: five lots is floor-level coverage, the thinnest sample on this list alongside Person. The price is a real number; the selection is not yet a real market. Treat this county as open for requests — name the town and we sweep it directly.

knowledge.title: Sampson County — what the money buys
knowledge.html:
Sampson County

Sampson is volume-acreage country: about $10,700 an acre around Clinton, 70 to 90 minutes out. Ten-acre and twenty-acre tracts price here the way single lots price in Johnston. The one thing to know: you are buying into a working farm economy. Hog operations and spray fields are part of the landscape, and they are protected agriculture, not a nuisance you can zone away. Drive the road, roll the windows down, and visit on a warm afternoon before you sign anything.

knowledge.title: What this list does NOT cover (honest gaps)
knowledge.html:
• Wake is understated: 21 lots, and 20 of them came from a single portal. Eight of eight major land portals (Zillow, Realtor.com, Redfin, LandWatch, Land.com, LandSearch, LandsOfAmerica, LandFlip) blocked automated collection with hard 403s, and the stealth-proxy fallback was out of credits. Wake re-sweep is the top queued fix; if that one portal blocks tomorrow, Wake coverage drops to one lot.
  • Johnston is understated for the same reason: 28 lots against Harnett's 43 inverts the real-world ordering. Johnston is closer to Raleigh, faster-growing, and carries more raw-land supply across its dozen towns.
  • Lee County has one lot. Sanford was never swept as its own unit, and one lot wedged between Harnett (43), Chatham (28), and Moore (11) is a collection gap, not a market fact. Edgecombe, Pitt, and Randolph also sit at one lot each, on the outer edge of the ring where thin is at least plausible.
  • Zero coverage inside the 90-minute ring: Warren, Halifax, Northampton, Greene, Lenoir, Duplin, and eastern Guilford have no rows at all. Warren is the sharpest miss — it borders three of the richest-covered counties in the set (Vance, Franklin, Granville) and cannot genuinely be empty.
  • Person was never deliberately swept. Its four to six rows arrived mislabeled as Durham and were re-filed after parcel checks. The accidental rows prove Person inventory exists and is reachable; the dedicated pass has not happened.
  • Eleven rows carry unresolved county labels: eight harvested as Durham that Durham parcel GIS could not confirm, plus rows flagged probable Person or possibly Orange. Granville arrived split across four label variants and merges to roughly 55 lots.
  • Cross-county mislabeling measured roughly 10% on the one source that verified every listing description — 3 hard errors in 31 candidates, concentrated in Zebulon, Wendell, Fuquay-Varina, and Holly Springs. The other ~360 rows got no per-listing description check, so some lots filed as Johnston, Harnett, or Franklin are Wake lots wearing the wrong label, which understates Wake further.
  • Five verification batches ran degraded. Alongside the 370 verified-live lots, 115 remain unverified and 67 carry stale-risk status; 10 dead listings were killed and removed.
  • Facebook Marketplace and Craigslist FSBO land cannot be collected by automation — login walls and bot detection — and both carry real for-sale-by-owner volume. The eight walled portals above are equally unreachable by machine. These channels need a human pass.
  • Off-market channels are identified but not yet harvested: county GIS vacant-parcel screens (present-use-value deferred-tax tracts with near-zero building value), Clerk of Court tax-foreclosure and upset-bid calendars, and municipal surplus-property lists. Wake's active foreclosure docket currently skews toward houses, not raw land.
  • All prices are asking prices. No closed-sale data calibrates them, and lots that sold fast never appear in a harvest like this — the sample skews toward what lingers on market.
  • Single-digit samples set the median in Wayne (5), Person (5), Wilson (8), and Nash (9). Those medians price the county roughly; they do not map it.
  • County-guide drive times are corridor-level estimates from geography. Per-lot drive times exist only where the listing row carries one.
